teaching.task: A class prepares pentyl ethanoate, the banana-smelling ester, and gets about 60% of the most it could make. Is that a failed practical? How do you prepare an ester safely, calculate its yield, explain what limits it, and design a fair test of whether excess acid helps?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) 60%: fail or not? (1); (2) the aim and the limiting reactant (2); (3) reflux to approach equilibrium without losing volatile liquids; why a mantle (3); (4) one variable changed, the work-up kept identical (4); (5) get the ester out and weigh it, recalled in one pass (5); (6) percentage yield from moles of the limiting reactant (6); (7) the equilibrium ceiling and work-up losses (7); (8) repeats agree, and the difference between ratios is larger than the spread (8); (9) a correctly weighed dry, pure product gives a correct yield; a wet product reads too high; what the comparison can and cannot show (9); (10) identify the product without sniffing it (10); (11) hazards and controls (11); memory aid (12); attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: a class makes pentyl ethanoate, the banana-smelling ester, and gets about sixty per cent of the most it could make, so the practical asks whether that is a failed practical, what limits the yield and how to measure it fairly. The aim asks whether excess ethanoic acid raises the yield; the acid and alcohol react one to one, so the alcohol is the limiting reactant and sets the most ester any group could make. The mixture is heated under reflux with anti-bumping granules after the teacher adds a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as the catalyst, and the variables card holds the mole ratio, the percentage yield and everything kept the same. The ester is separated in a separating funnel, washed with sodium hydrogen carbonate solution, dried and weighed. The yield is worked one stage at a time from moles of pentan-1-ol to the most ester possible and then the percentage. Equilibrium sets a ceiling below a hundred per cent and losses on glassware, in the washes and on the drying agent take it lower; three groups per ratio agree closely and the gap between ratios is much bigger than the spread. A dry, pure product gives an accurate yield, and a matched work-up keeps the comparison valid. The memory aid is equilibrium sets the ceiling, the work-up decides how close you get. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Warm pentan-1-ol with ethanoic acid and a little concentrated sulfuric acid, and you make pentyl ethanoate, an ester that smells like bananas. A class makes it and gets about sixty per cent of the most it could make. Is that a failed practical? Not necessarily. Let's see what limits the yield, and how to test fairly whether you can raise it.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student heated 3.70 g of butan-1-ol with excess ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid under reflux. After washing and drying the product, she collected 3.19 g of butyl ethanoate. (a) Calculate the percentage yield of butyl ethanoate. (b) Explain TWO reasons why the yield is less than 100%." (4 marks.) Molar masses on the card: butan-1-ol 74.12 g mol⁻¹; butyl ethanoate 116.16 g mol⁻¹. New alcohol and ester. Answer: n(butan-1-ol) = 3.70 ÷ 74.12 = 0.0499 mol; 1:1, so the maximum n(ester) = 0.0499 mol; maximum mass = 0.0499 × 116.16 = 5.80 g; yield = 3.19 ÷ 5.80 × 100 = 55.0%. Reasons: the reaction is reversible and reaches equilibrium, so not all the alcohol reacts; ester is lost during transfers, washing and drying. Crossed mistake: "3.19 ÷ 3.70 × 100 = 86%" (dividing masses directly, the moles step skipped). (A2) "A student prepared propyl ethanoate from propan-1-ol and excess ethanoic acid. She ran off the water layer from the separating funnel and weighed the ester layer straight away, without washing or drying it. She calculated a percentage yield of 104%. Explain why her result is inaccurate, and describe TWO changes to her method that would give a more accurate yield." (3 marks.) Answer: more than 100% means the weighed liquid contained substances other than ester (water, and probably leftover ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol), so the mass and yield are too high; wash with sodium hydrogen carbonate solution (then water), dry with anhydrous magnesium sulfate, and if possible distil, collecting near the ester's boiling point, before weighing. Crossed mistake: "Over 100%, so the reaction went to completion" (even complete conversion caps the yield at 100%, and esterification stops at equilibrium).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the production, in a school laboratory, of simple esters" "describe the procedures required to safely handle and dispose of organic substances (ACSCH075)" (carried by the risk table, route review change 5) this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the investigation; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: the aim (does excess ethanoic acid raise the yield of pentyl ethanoate?); the alcohol setting the theoretical maximum in both ratios; the reflux set-up with an electric heating mantle (and why a water bath is not hot enough for this mixture); the variables; the work-up in one pass (water, sodium hydrogen carbonate wash with venting, drying, weighing in a weighed vial); the percentage yield from moles of the limiting reactant; the equilibrium ceiling and work-up losses; reliability from class repeats; what makes an isolated yield accurate, and what the ratio comparison can and cannot support; the "over 100%" warning sign; identifying the product (a separate layer, no fizz, the boiling point if distilled, wafting only); the risk assessment and disposal. Recalled, not re-taught: the equation, names and conditions; why the reaction stops short; why excess reactant shifts it right; why each wash works; why the ester boils low (all chem-m7-c10); validity, reliability, accuracy, word, feature, fix (skills-s07, chem-m7-p03); moles and molar mass (Year 11). Not here: the K expression, the equilibrium calculation and any numerical ceiling (author note d, Revision 2); removing water continuously (c10 author note c); acid hydrolysis and saponification (c12); spectroscopy (Module 8); multi-step synthesis (c13).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c10: the ester group ringed red; the acid side soft amber and the alcohol side pale blue only when a structure is shown; water in the Module 5 water colour; the two ratios in fixed colours across chips, bars and dots (1:1 grey-blue, 2:1 teal); the equilibrium ceiling a dashed navy line; losses hatched terracotta; hazards terracotta, controls green. Board layout (three zones, constant, as chem-m7-p03 and p04): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus plate; the right third holds the current card (method step, variables, calculation strip, yield ladder, validity card, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every label dims when its sentence ends. Plates and owner rules: no people or hands (liquids are measured by coded pours into painted glassware; the teacher's addition of acid is a coded dropper outline; the funnel's venting is a coded arrow); apparatus as painted plates, listed by filename, never stretched; structures coded in the c10 style; at most about three bright text items; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (about 15 to 30 s) with one crossed-out mistake; original HSC-style questions only; real GHS classifications; school rules checked against NSW Chemical Safety in Schools (sources in "Safety facts check"); Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims; optional key notes hold. No human figures.
